reasoning rather than code, but where data exist (Case 4) I add a short analysis in both languages.

# Exercise 1 — Possible predictor variables for Cases 3 and 4

*For Cases 3 and 4 in Section 1.5, list possible predictor variables that might be useful,
assuming the relevant data are available.*

## Case 3 — resale value of leased vehicles

| Group | Candidate predictors |
|---|---|
| The vehicle | make, model, body type, engine size, fuel type, transmission, colour, options/trim level |
| Its use | odometer reading at sale, age at sale (lease length), accident and service history, condition grade |
| The lease | lessee type (private vs. corporate fleet), region where it was used |
| The market | new-car price of the same model, whether the model has been replaced or facelifted, used-car supply, fuel prices, interest rates, consumer confidence, exchange rate (affects import prices), season/month of sale |
| The sale | sales channel (auction vs. dealer), location of sale |

## Case 4 — weekly air passengers by route and class

| Group | Candidate predictors |
|---|---|
| Calendar | school holidays in each city (they differ by state), public holidays, Easter/Christmas, week of year |
| Events | major sporting events, conferences and festivals (and which city hosts them), strikes |
| Price & product | own ticket prices by class, competitors' prices, seat capacity per class (the reclassification trial), number of flights / aircraft size |
| Competition | entry/exit of competing (cut-price) airlines, competitor capacity |
| Marketing | advertising campaigns, loyalty-programme promotions |
| Economy | GDP / business activity (business class), consumer confidence, fuel prices, exchange rate (tourism) |

### Supporting analysis: what the `melsyd` data show {.tabset .tabset-pills}

The weekly Ansett Melbourne–Sydney series shows why several of these predictors matter:
the 1989 pilots' strike (zero traffic), the 1992 seat reclassification (economy falls while
business rises), missing values, and a strong holiday effect at the start of each year.

#### R

```{r ex1-melsyd}
autoplot(melsyd[, "Economy.Class"]) +
  ggtitle("Economy class passengers: Melbourne–Sydney") + xlab("Year") + ylab("Thousands")

# Quantify the events: weekly mean per year and number of missing / zero weeks
econ <- melsyd[, "Economy.Class"]
yearly <- data.frame(year = floor(time(econ)), econ = as.numeric(econ))
aggregate(econ ~ year, data = yearly, FUN = function(v) round(mean(v), 1))
c(missing_weeks = sum(is.na(econ)), zero_weeks = sum(econ == 0, na.rm = TRUE))
```

#### Python

```{python ex1-melsyd-py}
melsyd = fpp.load("melsyd")
econ = melsyd["Economy.Class"]
econ.attrs = dict(melsyd.attrs)
fpp.autoplot(econ, title="Economy class passengers: Melbourne–Sydney", xlab="Year", ylab="Thousands")
plt.show()

yearly = pd.DataFrame({"year": np.floor(fpp.ts_time(econ)).astype(int), "econ": econ.to_numpy()})
print(yearly.groupby("year")["econ"].mean().round(1))
print({"missing_weeks": int(econ.isna().sum()), "zero_weeks": int((econ == 0).sum())})
```

# Exercise 2 — The five steps for Case 3

*For Case 3 in Section 1.5, describe the five steps of forecasting in the context of this project.*

1. **Problem definition.** Forecast the resale value of each leased vehicle at the end of its
   three-year lease, so the company can price leases and control profit. Agree with management
   on the unit (each vehicle), horizon (3 years ahead), accuracy measure (e.g. MAE in dollars)
   and how the forecasts will be used (lease pricing, fleet purchase decisions, sales timing).
   Bring the resale specialists in early — their cooperation is part of the problem.
2. **Gathering information.** Collect the company's historical records of purchased vehicles
   and their eventual resale prices, plus vehicle attributes, usage (km, condition) and market
   data (new-car prices, used-car indices, fuel prices, interest rates). Capture the
   specialists' knowledge of what drives prices (e.g. model changes, colour preferences).
3. **Preliminary (exploratory) analysis.** Plot resale value against age, kilometres, make and
   model; look for trends over time (e.g. falling values of large cars), seasonality in sale
   prices, outliers (damaged vehicles) and strong relationships between predictors.
4. **Choosing and fitting models.** Compare a few candidates — e.g. a regression model of resale
   value on vehicle and market predictors (Chapter 5), possibly with time-series terms for the
   market trend (Chapter 9), against a simple benchmark such as "same depreciation rate as similar
   vehicles last year". Use training/test splits by sale date.
5. **Using and evaluating the model.** Produce resale forecasts (with prediction intervals) for every
   vehicle as it is leased; once vehicles are sold, compare forecasts with actual prices, monitor
   accuracy by make/model, and re-estimate regularly. Present results in a way that supports the
   specialists rather than threatening them.

*(Conceptual exercise — no code required.)*

*Reference: Hyndman, R.J., & Athanasopoulos, G. (2018). Forecasting: Principles and Practice
(2nd ed.). OTexts. <https://otexts.com/fpp2/>*
